entry: Census region of the southern United States, also called Dixie or the South. It is the largest of the four census regions, with about 126 million residents as of 2020. Historically defined as the states south of the 18th-century Mason–Dixon line, the [[Ohio River|Ohio River]] and the 36°30′ parallel, it includes subregions such as the Southeast, South Central, Upper South and Deep South. The region's history was shaped by [[Slavery|slavery]], the [[Reconstruction era]] and Jim Crow segregation, which lasted into the 1960s. It contains almost all of the [[Bible Belt]], an area of high Protestant church attendance, and it is the fastest-growing U.S. region of the 21st century. [[Houston]] is its largest city.

Low-cost airline of the United States, headquartered in [[Dallas]], Texas. It was established on March 9, 1967, by Herb Kelleher and Rollin King as Air Southwest Co., and in 1971 it began operating as an intrastate airline wholly within Texas, first flying between Dallas, Houston and San Antonio. Regional interstate service began in 1979. Its fleet is entirely [[Boeing 737]] aircraft, and it uses a point-to-point system with a rolling-hub model rather than hub-and-spoke. Southwest serves over 100 destinations, including [[Puerto Rico]], [[Mexico]], Central America and the [[Caribbean]]. As of 2024 it was the fourth-largest airline in North America by passengers carried.

Catholic lay religious order of a military, chivalric and noble nature, with headquarters in [[Rome]]. It has no national territory but is considered a sovereign entity under [[International law|international law]]. It traces its continuity to the [[Knights Hospitaller]], a chivalric order founded about 1099 in the [[Kingdom of Jerusalem]], and it is led by an elected prince and grand master. The order maintains diplomatic relations with 115 states, issues its own passports, and has been a United Nations General Assembly observer since 1994. Its humanitarian work includes aid to refugees, to victims of [[Natural disaster|natural disasters]], epidemics and war.

State having [[Sovereignty|sovereignty]], the highest authority over a defined territory. A sovereign state is generally considered independent and must have a permanent population, a defined territory, a government not under the control of another, and the capacity to interact with other sovereign states. Recognition by other states plays an important role in determining its status, and unrecognized states often have difficulty conducting diplomatic relations. Westphalian sovereignty, based on territoriality and the absence of external agents in domestic affairs, began with the [[Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648. More than 200 sovereign states exist, most of them represented in the [[United Nations]]. Disputes over Taiwan or [[Kosovo]] show the tension between legal criteria and political realities.

Supreme, independent control and lawmaking authority over a territory. Sovereignty is expressed through the power to rule and make law, and it entails hierarchy within a state as well as external autonomy in international affairs. It is assigned to the person, body or institution with ultimate authority over a state's citizens. A state is generally considered sovereign over a territory when it has consistently exercised authority there without objection from other states. De jure sovereignty is the legal right to rule; de facto sovereignty is the factual ability to do so. Stephen D. Krasner distinguished domestic, interdependence, international legal and [[Peace of Westphalia|Westphalian]] sovereignty. The term entered English in the 14th century. [[Thomas Hobbes]] advanced the idea in *Leviathan* (1651).

Armed conflict in Afghanistan from December 1979 to February 1989. The [[Soviet Union]] and the Afghan government fought mujahideen rebels backed by Pakistan, the United States, China and Iran. Soviet forces held most large cities, while guerrillas fought in the countryside. The war killed between one and three million Afghans and drove millions more into refuge, mostly in Pakistan and Iran. Troop strength reached about 115,000 by the mid-1980s. [[Mikhail Gorbachev]] announced a complete withdrawal in mid-1987, and the last Soviet column left on February 15, 1989. Scholars cite the war as a significant factor in the Soviet Union's dissolution by 1991.

State space program of the Soviet Union, active from 1951 until the Soviet Union's dissolution in 1991. Divided among competing design bureaus and led in the 1950s by [[Sergei Korolev]], it launched [[Sputnik 1]], the first artificial satellite, in 1957, and carried Laika, the first animal in Earth orbit. [[Yuri Gagarin]] became the first human in space aboard [[Vostok 1]] in 1961, and [[Valentina Tereshkova]] became the first woman in space. The Salyut program (1971–1986) operated six crewed space stations, followed by [[Mir]] (1986–2000), the first modular station. The program's legacy includes Roscosmos' segment of the [[International Space Station]], the [[Soyuz (spacecraft)|Soyuz]] spacecraft and the GLONASS navigation system.

Series of student-led protests against apartheid in South Africa, beginning in Soweto on June 16, 1976. Students opposed the [[Afrikaans]] Medium Decree of 1974, which required Afrikaans instruction in some subjects at black schools, a language many regarded as the "language of the oppressor." Police fired on demonstrators, and 176 pupils were killed in Soweto by the end of June 16. Unrest spread across South Africa, with 575 deaths from violence by February 1977. The uprising revived domestic and international opposition to [[Apartheid|apartheid]]. June 16 is now Youth Day, a public holiday in South Africa.

Plant-based beverage made by soaking, grinding and boiling soybeans, originating in China. It is a stable emulsion of oil, water and protein, and it is an intermediate product in the manufacture of [[Tofu|tofu]]. Its use increased during the [[Qing dynasty]], when gentle heating for at least 90 minutes was found to break down compounds that can cause [[Flatulence|flatulence]]. It became a common beverage in Europe and North America in the latter half of the 20th century, and it substitutes for dairy milk for people who are vegan, lactose-intolerant or allergic to milk. Soy milk is also used to make soy yogurt, cheese analogues and other imitation dairy products. A 2017 ruling by the [[European Union|Court of Justice of the European Union]] held that such products may not be labeled "milk" or "cheese."

Liquid condiment of Chinese origin, traditionally made from fermented soybeans, roasted grain, brine and *Aspergillus* molds. It is recognized for its saltiness and [[Umami|umami]] taste. Soy sauce was created in its current form about 2,200 years ago during the Western Han dynasty. Originally a way to stretch [[Salt|salt]], an expensive commodity, it became a staple of East and Southeast Asian cooking. Buddhist practitioners who came to Japan from China in the 7th century introduced soy-based products, including shōyu, and the [[Dutch East India Company]] began exporting Japanese shoyu in 1647. Brewing in Korea may date to the Three Kingdoms era. Soy sauce is indefinitely shelf-stable and is often eaten with rice, noodles or [[Sushi|sushi]].

[[Legume|Legume]] native to East Asia, widely grown for its edible bean. Domesticated from the wild soybean (*Glycine soja*) in north-central [[China]] between 6,000 and 9,000 years ago, *Glycine max* is the world's most grown legume and an important animal feed. Its high protein and oil content make it a key food source, and soybean oil is widely used in cooking and industry. Traditional foods include edamame, [[Soy milk|soy milk]] and [[Tofu|tofu]], while fermented products include [[Soy sauce|soy sauce]], nattō and tempeh. Brazil and the United States lead modern production, and most soybeans are genetically modified, usually for insect, herbicide or drought resistance. About three-quarters of the crop feeds livestock. Rising demand for meat since the 1980s has contributed to [[Deforestation|deforestation]] in the Amazon.

Series of spacecraft in service since the 1960s, designed for the Soviet space program by the Korolev Design Bureau. The Soyuz has made more than 140 flights and was the sole means of crewed transport to the [[International Space Station]] between the Space Shuttle's 2011 retirement and the 2020 debut of SpaceX's Crew Dragon. It has three sections: an orbital module, a descent module where the crew sits for launch and return, and a service module. The orbital and service modules are discarded before reentry, which reduces weight and gives the crew more habitable space than the Apollo spacecraft. The Soyuz carries up to three crew members. Soyuz 1 failed in April 1967 when its parachute did not deploy, killing cosmonaut Vladimir Komarov. The design remains in use by Roscosmos.

American aerospace and artificial intelligence [[Conglomerate (company)|conglomerate]], headquartered in Starbase, Texas. Founded in 2002 by [[Elon Musk]] to reduce the cost of [[Spaceflight|spaceflight]], SpaceX built the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy [[Launch vehicle|launch vehicles]] and the Dragon spacecraft. It conducts more orbital launches each year than any other provider. Its Starlink satellite constellation provides broadband internet. In 2008, Falcon 1 became the first liquid-fueled rocket developed and launched to orbit by a private company. The company is credited with advances in reusable rockets. Its largest customers include [[NASA]].

Competition between the United States and the Soviet Union in spaceflight during the [[Cold War|Cold War]]. It grew out of the ballistic missile arms race that followed [[World War II]], and the technological advantage it showed was seen as essential to national security. The Soviet Union launched [[Sputnik 1]] on October 4, 1957, and sent [[Yuri Gagarin]] on an orbital flight on April 12, 1961. President [[John F. Kennedy]] then asked Congress in May 1961 to commit to landing a man on the Moon before the decade ended, a goal met by [[Apollo 11]] in July 1969. The Soviet N1 rocket failed to enable a crewed lunar landing and was canceled, and the Soviets concentrated on the Salyut space stations. A period of détente produced the July 1975 Apollo–Soyuz Test Project, and in 1993 the two nations agreed on the Shuttle–Mir and [[International Space Station]] programs.

Partially reusable low Earth orbital spacecraft system, operated by [[NASA]] from 1981 to 2011. Its official name was the Space Transportation System. The orbiter launched vertically with two solid rocket boosters and an external tank, and it landed as a glider. Five complete orbiters flew 135 missions. Operational flights launched satellites and interplanetary probes, deployed the [[Hubble Space Telescope]], and helped build and service the [[International Space Station]]. Two orbiters were lost in accidents, Challenger in 1986 and Columbia in 2003, killing 14 astronauts. The final flight, by Atlantis, ended on July 21, 2011. The United States then relied on the Russian [[Soyuz (spacecraft)|Soyuz]] spacecraft to reach the station until 2020. Launches took place from the [[Kennedy Space Center]] in Florida.

Fatal failure of the [[Space Shuttle]] Challenger, which broke apart 73 seconds after launch on January 28, 1986. The orbiter disintegrated about 46,000 feet above the Atlantic Ocean, killing all seven crew members, including schoolteacher Christa McAuliffe. The cause was the failure of O-ring seals in a joint of the right solid rocket booster, which had stiffened in record-low launch-morning temperatures. Test data since 1977 had shown the flaw, and [[NASA]] managers disregarded engineers' warnings. President [[Ronald Reagan]] created the Rogers Commission, which criticized NASA's decision-making. The disaster caused a 32-month hiatus in the Space Shuttle program.

Destruction of the [[Space Shuttle]] orbiter Columbia during reentry on February 1, 2003, killing all seven astronauts on mission STS-107. Foam insulation that broke off the external tank during launch had damaged the thermal protection on the left wing. Hot atmospheric gases entered the wing during reentry and destroyed its internal structure, and the orbiter broke apart over [[Texas]] and [[Louisiana]]. Shuttle flights were suspended for more than two years, and construction of the [[International Space Station]] paused until July 2005. Afterward, flights went only to the station, where crews could shelter if reentry was unsafe, except for one Hubble repair mission.

Habitable artificial satellite that remains in orbit and hosts humans for extended periods. Most space stations have served as research laboratories, though some have had military or commercial uses, including hosting space tourists. The first was Salyut 1, launched by the Soviet Union in 1971, followed by [[Skylab]] (1973) and [[Mir]], occupied from 1987. Human presence in orbit has been continuous since the transition from Mir to the [[International Space Station]], first occupied in 2000. China's [[Tiangong space station|Tiangong]] has been occupied since June 2022. The record for most people on all stations at once is 17, reached on May 30, 2023.

Vehicle designed to fly and operate in outer space. Spacecraft serve purposes including communications, Earth observation, meteorology, navigation, planetary exploration and the transport of humans and cargo. Most require a [[Launch vehicle|launch vehicle]] to reach space. Most orbital spacecraft are not recoverable, while recoverable designs may be reusable, like the [[SpaceX]] Dragon and the [[Space Shuttle]] orbiters, or expendable, like the [[Soyuz (spacecraft)|Soyuz]]. The first artificial satellite, [[Sputnik 1]], was launched by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957. The first crewed spacecraft, [[Vostok 1]], carried [[Yuri Gagarin]] in 1961. As of 2026, only three nations have flown crewed spacecraft: the Soviet Union or Russia, the United States and China.

Mathematical model in physics combining three dimensions of space and one of time into a single four-dimensional continuum. Until the turn of the 20th century, space and time were assumed to be distinct. In 1908, Hermann Minkowski presented a geometric interpretation of [[Special relativity|special relativity]] that fused time and space into Minkowski space, which proved vital to [[General relativity|general relativity]]. In special relativity, the rate at which time passes for an object depends on its velocity relative to an observer. A point in spacetime is an event specified by four coordinates, and the path of a particle through spacetime is its world line. In general relativity, spacetime is curved by mass and energy, and gravitational fields can slow the passage of time. Gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime, were detected in 2015.

Brand of canned, precooked lunch meat of pork and ham, made by Hormel Foods Corporation. Introduced in the United States in 1937, it became a staple of U.S. military rations in [[World War II]], with over 150 million pounds received by the military before the war ended. It was introduced to Guam, Hawaii and the Philippines, where it was absorbed into local diets. Ingredients include pork, ham, salt, modified potato starch, sugar and [[Sodium nitrite|sodium nitrite]]. As of 2022 it was sold in 48 countries. A [[Monty Python]] sketch that repeated the name helped give "spam" its meaning of unsolicited electronic messages.

Armed conflict between the United States and [[Spain]], fought from April 21 to August 13, 1898. It began after a mysterious explosion sank the USS Maine in [[Havana]] Harbor on February 15, 1898. The war was fought in the Caribbean and the Pacific, where U.S. naval power proved decisive. American forces destroyed the Spanish fleet at [[Manila|Manila Bay]] on May 1 and captured Santiago de Cuba in July. Under the Treaty of Paris, signed December 10, 1898, Spain ceded [[Puerto Rico]], [[Guam]] and the [[Philippines]] to the United States. Cuba was set to become independent in 1902 but in practice became a U.S. protectorate. The war ended almost four centuries of Spanish presence in the Americas, Asia and the Pacific.

Series of early 19th-century conflicts that ended Spanish rule across most of mainland Spanish America. They began with the 1808 Spanish uprising against the French invasion under [[Napoleon]], which left the Spanish Crown vacant and prompted colonial juntas to rule in the king's name. Attempts at reconstruction failed from 1810, and the wars developed into secessionist struggles in which Royalists fought Patriots. [[Simón Bolívar]] secured Venezuela and New Granada by 1821, and the patriot victory at Ayacucho in 1824 was decisive. The new republics abandoned the [[Inquisition]] and noble titles, though slavery was abolished only in the 1850s in most countries. Cuba and Puerto Rico remained under Spanish rule until the [[Spanish–American War]]. Spain formally recognized the losses only in 1836.

Conflict fought in Spain from 1936 to 1939 between the Republicans and the Nationalist rebels. The Republicans were loyal to the left-leaning Popular Front government of the Second Spanish Republic and included socialists, anarchists and communists; they received support from the [[Soviet Union]] and Mexico. The Nationalists, an alliance of Falangists, monarchists and conservatives, were aided by [[Italy]] and [[Nazi Germany]]. [[Francisco Franco]] was appointed supreme leader on 1 October 1936 and emerged as the primary Nationalist leader. Franco entered [[Madrid]] and declared victory on 1 April 1939, and the Nationalists ruled Spain until his death in November 1975. Both sides committed atrocities, and hundreds of thousands of Republicans fled to refugee camps, mostly in southern France.

System of tribunals established in 1478 to enforce Catholic orthodoxy in Spain. Authorized by Pope Sixtus IV and organized by the Catholic Monarchs, [[Ferdinand II of Aragon]] and [[Isabella I of Castile]], it became an effective instrument of state power. It prosecuted an estimated 150,000 people, of whom 3,000–5,000 were executed, mostly by burning at the stake, particularly in its first 50 years. Other punishments included penance, flogging, exile and imprisonment, and victims' property was often confiscated. Royal decrees of 1492 and 1502 ordered [[Jews]] and [[Muslims]] to convert or leave, and an estimated 40,000–100,000 Jews were expelled in 1492. Its targets later included Protestants, [[Witchcraft|witchcraft]] and Freemasonry.
